content:
How to talk to your employer about rheumatoid arthritis at work is a question that many people delay — and understandably so. But disclosure, approached strategically, typically leads to better outcomes than struggling silently.

Quick answer: When talking to your employer about RA: focus on functional impact not diagnosis, propose specific adjustments (flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, WFH on flare days), follow up in writing. Under the Equality Act 2010, reasonable adjustments are a legal requirement. ACAS (0300 123 1100) provides free advice.

Your Legal Rights

Under the Equality Act 2010, RA qualifies as a disability if it has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on day-to-day activities. Your employer has a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments. Refusing to do so is disability discrimination.

Preparing for the Conversation

  1. Choose the right setting — request a private meeting with your line manager or HR, framed as a "health and work meeting."
  2. Focus on function, not diagnosis — "I have difficulty typing for extended periods due to hand stiffness" is more actionable than naming the condition.
  3. Come with solutions — propose specific adjustments rather than presenting a problem without suggestions.
  4. Follow up in writing — email a summary of what was agreed within 24 hours.

Reasonable Adjustments to Request

  • Flexible start/finish times for morning stiffness
  • Work from home on high-pain days
  • Ergonomic keyboard, mouse, chair and desk setup
  • Reserved accessible parking
  • Regular short breaks to move and stretch
  • Phased return to work after flares

Q&A

Question: Am I legally required to disclose my RA to my employer?
Short answer: No — but without disclosure your employer cannot make adjustments. Disclosure is in your interests if adjustments would help you work more effectively.

Question: What if my employer refuses adjustments?
Short answer: Contact ACAS (0300 123 1100) for free conciliation. If discrimination persists, you can raise an Employment Tribunal claim.

Practical next steps for How to Talk to Your Employer About Rheumatoid Arthritis at Work

If you came here about How to Talk to Your Employer About Rheumatoid Arthritis at Work, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Quick questions about Talk Your Employer About

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep expectations kind while you work on how to talk to your employer about rheumatoid arthritis at work. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
